“You made the right call,” Lucas said softly, though a tremor of guilt frayed his words. “The militia had the entire street sealed. Even if I was on my feet, we wouldn't have made it ten yards. Surrendering was the only reason we're still breathing.”

Mina opened her eyes. She started to speak, but the words caught in her throat as the telepathic link between them hummed. Across the bond, she caught the chilling undercurrent of Lucas’s thoughts—not cold logic, but a suffocating, freezing dread. He was staring at the iron on his wrists, fighting off the ghosts of the laboratory. The sheer weight of his terror washed over her, and the restless frustration in her chest softened. His steady, calculating presence pushed back against her frantic pulse, grounding her even as her own warmth reached out to anchor him.

She leaned closer, letting her shoulder brush his. “I know,” she murmured, her voice quiet and gentle now. “I hate being locked in. But we’re alive. We'll figure this out together.”

Hours dragged past in an agonizing, slow drip. The faint, muffled echoes of dwarven voices reverberated through the thick walls, a constant reminder of the massive bureaucratic machine operating above them. Finally, the heavy deadbolt cracked open. A dwarf clad in simple, austere gray robes stepped into the chamber. His face was a blank slate of official detachment.

“You are being separated,” the official announced, his tone flat and unyielding.

“Separated?” Lucas demanded, his chains rattling as he took a sharp step forward. “Why?”

The official gestured to the guards waiting in the corridor. “Orders from the High Council. You will wait in separate cells until you are called before the magistrates.”

Mina tensed, her fists clenching as she stepped back, ready to fight them off, but Thomas caught her shoulder. “Don’t,” he said, his voice low and steady. “They want to see if our stories match. They’re looking for a reason to doubt us. Just keep your head.”

Lucas felt his heart hammer against his ribs, cold sweat breaking across his skin. “We don't need to rehearse the truth,” he said tightly, though the thought of being locked in a dark room alone made his chest tighten with dread.

The dwarven guards stepped in, grabbing their arms with rough, heavy hands. Mina threw a desperate glance back at Lucas and Thomas as they pulled her toward a descending stairwell, but the thick timber door slammed shut, cutting them off from each other.

Lucas was dragged down a separate, dark hallway and shoved into a cramped stone cell. The iron grate slammed shut, the heavy lock turning with a cold, hollow thud. The walls were rough bedrock, with no windows and no way out. A single, dim crystal in the ceiling flickered weakly, casting pale shadows across a narrow stone cot.

The silence in the cell was suffocating.

Lucas stumbled backward, his breath catching in his throat as panic clawed at his chest. The rough stone walls seemed to blur, shifting in the dim light until they looked like the polished steel and glass of the laboratory in Kingston. He could feel the phantom sting of needles in his arms, the freezing cold of the metal table beneath his back, and the sound of the researcher’s pen scratching across a clipboard while he lay helpless in the dark.

He clamped his chained hands over his ears and dropped to his knees on the freezing floor. He forced himself to count, running through numbers and equations in his head just to drown out the screaming memory. He pressed his palms flat against the stone, focusing on the cold, gritty texture beneath his skin, fighting with everything he had to stay grounded in the present.

Across the lower holding tiers, Mina paced her cell like a caged animal. The small space made her skin crawl. Every instinct screamed at her to break the iron bars and run, to find open air and break into a sprint. Frustrated and desperate for release, she kicked the heavy wall; the jolt sent a sharp ache up her leg, but did nothing to ease the tight, suffocating panic in her chest.

She slumped against the cold iron bars, breathing hard as she touched the rough, blood-soaked bandages wrapped around her arm.

A faint rustle of smooth cloth against stone broke the quiet.

“You hold allies in the dark.”

The voice was a low whisper, slipping through the narrow gap between the cell door and the stone floor. Mina froze, her green eyes widening. She dropped into a silent crouch, pressing her ear close to the cold iron.

“Who's there?” Mina hissed, her voice sharp with suspicion.

A quiet chuckle vibrated through the stone—a rough, forced sound that tried to mimic the deep gravel of a dwarf. But beneath the scratching tone, Mina caught the steady, measured breath of an outsider trying to hide their natural cadence—the smooth, controlled lilt of an elf or a polished tongue from the Central Lands. “Names are a luxury the hunted cannot afford. I come with a warning. The High Council is tearing itself apart. Some demand your heads to appease the Central Lands, while others see you as the hammer they need to crush the Unbound. Your trial is just a show.”

Mina’s jaw tightened. “What do you want from us?”

“Only that you stay alive,” the voice murmured, the refined accent slipping through before dying away into the dark corridor. “When the magistrates cast their stones, do not flinch. The winds are already shifting in your favor.”

The shadow vanished from beneath the door, leaving Mina alone with the quiet echo of the warning.

Down in the deepest holding cells, Thomas sat on the edge of his stone cot. He didn’t pace, and he didn’t let the cold gloom of the dungeon wear him down. He simply closed his eyes, letting his breathing slow to a calm, steady rhythm. He turned the coming interrogation over in his mind, bracing himself. He knew the council would try to use their exhaustion against them, pushing until they broke. But Thomas had spent his life standing his ground. When the dwarven judges tried to hammer them, they would find nothing to shatter.

The heavy clatter of armored boots broke the silence. The iron door creaked open, revealing two dwarven guards.

“The High Council demands your presence,” the lead guard grunted.

Thomas rose to his full height, his broad shoulders easily dwarfing the sentinels. “Lead the way.”

The Council Chamber of Brum’korath was a staggering architectural marvel, engineered specifically to crush the ego of anyone standing in its center. The vaulted ceiling soared hundreds of feet into the darkness, illuminated by massive, glowing veins of raw aetherium that pulsed like the heartbeat of a sleeping god. Colossal statues of ancient dwarven warlords lined the perimeter, their stone faces judging the room with uncompromising severity.

In the center of the vast chamber sat a massive, semicircular table carved from a single slab of black granite. Seated behind it were the Elders of Brum’korath, their expressions locked into masks of absolute authority.

Lucas was marched into the center of the floor, his chains echoing sharply against the stone. He immediately located Mina and Thomas, flanked by heavy guards near the center of the chamber. The relief of seeing them alive and upright provided a momentary surge of warmth, though the heavy bruises and weariness etched into their faces mirrored his own exhaustion.

Their eyes met across the floor. Thomas caught Lucas’s gaze, offering a subtle, unyielding nod that anchored the room's mounting dread. Beside him, Mina’s green eyes sharpened. The moment their sightlines locked, she reached across the open air, her telepathic presence brushing against Lucas’s mind like a warm, urgent current.

Someone came to my door in the cells, Mina projected, her thoughts carrying a sharp, restless edge. An outsider whispering through the gap, faking a rough dwarven drawl. They said this trial is a complete sham. The council is split right down the middle—half the elders want to hand us over to the Central Lands, and the other half want to use us as a sledgehammer against the Unbound. The voice told me to stay alive and stand our ground, that someone is moving in the shadows to tip the scales for us.

Lucas absorbed the data, his mind instantly mapping the hidden angles of the courtroom. An unseen hand playing the margins, he answered across the bond, drawing steady strength from her presence. We hold our ground and give them nothing to exploit.

Mina offered a faint, weary pulse of agreement. Thomas, reading the sudden, subtle hardening in their postures, shifted his weight and squared his broad shoulders, forming a unified, stoic front before the dais.

At the direct apex of the table sat Elder Valka. Her silver hair was tightly braided, and her piercing, ice-blue eyes scanned the three teenagers with the lethal calculation of a raptor. Seated to her immediate left was Elder Gorla, a heavily scarred dwarf clad in austere, unadorned council plate devoid of any factional heraldry. Gorla maintained a rigid, unreadable facade, but Lucas detected a microscopic shift in her posture—a faint, heavily suppressed tension.

Elder Valka raised a heavy, iron-bound gavel and struck the granite slab. The resulting concussive boom instantly silenced the sprawling chamber.

“Lucas, Mina, Thomas,” Elder Valka pronounced, her voice cold and commanding, echoing with heavy authority across the vaulted stone. “You stand before the high council of Brum’korath. You are charged with trespassing onto sovereign dwarven soil without permit, bringing violence into our streets, harboring among religious fanatics, and participating in a catastrophe that shattered our outer tiers. Yet our captains confirm your direct hand in slaying the beast that breached our gates. Your deeds stand in stark conflict.”

She paused, resting her heavy, ringed fingers upon a slate ledger set into the granite bench. “The preliminary accounting of your battle is written in blood and ruin. The eastern residential sectors have collapsed into the lower caverns. The municipal aqueduct hub lies fractured, drowning our secondary mine shafts. Forty-seven militia guards—including Captain Throm of the Iron Gate—perished holding the line. Two master engineers of the Stonemasons' Guild were crushed beneath falling colonnades, and over two hundred civilians remain buried in the rubble of the market tier. Our search crews continue to pull bodies from the dark, and the final toll will climb for days.”

Valka leaned forward, clasping her hands on the granite. “You will state your defense. Do not attempt to hide your guilt or weave falsehoods before this stone. Our justice is absolute, and our patience has been ground to dust.”

Lucas stepped forward, forcing his posture to remain rigidly upright despite the heavy iron binding his wrists. He drew upon his chilling, calculated focus, stripping his voice of all emotional resonance to deliver a cold, measured defense.

“We did not come to bring ruin to your mountain,” Lucas stated quietly, his dark eyes locking onto Valka. “We arrived as refugees seeking shelter, not conflict. Whatever fell from your skies was not summoned by the cult, and it was not a beast native to these rocks. It came with a targeted hostility, tearing through your gates to corner us. We did not choose that battlefield. We fought because retreat was impossible, and we brought it down through desperate improvisation alongside your own militia. If we had turned our backs, that creature would still be grinding this hall to dust.”

A stout, fiery-eyed elder sitting to Valka’s right slammed his fist on the table. “You admit you brought the beast to our gates! You harbored among fanatics who actively defy our laws! Your very presence is a poison to this mountain!”

Lucas maintained his cold, steady gaze. “The cult offered us shelter when the World Police hunted us like animals. We do not answer for the feuds between your factions. We answer only for the beast we slew.”

Mina surged forward, the heavy chains clanking violently against the stone floor. Her green eyes burned with a feral, untamed heat that directly challenged the crushing authority of the room.

“I have walked through the ash of your streets,” Mina declared, her voice a vibrant, rushing current that refused to be silenced. “I saw your people crushed under the rubble. We didn't turn our backs on them. We fought shoulder-to-shoulder with your militia, bleeding alongside them to crack that monster open. You want to label us criminals because you are terrified of the power we wield. Judge us for the damage, but do not pretend you would still have a city standing if we hadn't stepped into the fire.”

Her raw, untamed defiance caused a visible ripple of unease among the elders. Elder Valka’s eyes narrowed into dangerous, icy slits, but before she could drop the hammer of her authority, Thomas stepped into the absolute center of the floor.

Thomas anchored his stance with the unyielding density of solid bedrock. His broad shoulders squared, his heavy physical presence commanding the floor and shielding the space around his friends.

“You are analyzing the wrong battlefield,” Thomas rumbled, his voice a slow, tectonic vibration that demanded absolute attention from every dwarf in the chamber. “You are debating gang wars and property damage. The Disciple was not a rogue monster. It was a targeted weapon.”

Elder Valka leaned back, her severe features tightening. “A weapon deployed by whom?”

Thomas met her gaze, refusing to flinch under the massive weight of the council. He dropped the ultimate, devastating truth with the blunt force of a falling anvil.

“The Central Galactic Empire.”

The entire council chamber fractured into stunned, chaotic silence. The name was an ancient, terrifying ghost story—a cosmic boogeyman that had been buried in myth and restricted archives for over a millennium. The sheer audacity of invoking the Empire sent a shockwave of profound dread rippling through the elders.

Valka struck the granite slab furiously with her gavel, demanding order. Her face was pale, her voice vibrating with aggressive suspicion. “The Empire has not been recorded on this terrestrial plane for seventeen centuries! You dare stand in the Justice Hall and weave ancient fairytales to excuse your destruction?”

“It is not a fairytale,” Thomas replied, his stance an immovable monolith. “That beast was an advance strike—a Disciple sent to test this ground. Condemning us for the shattered stone will not alter the reality of what breached your gates. The Empire deployed that weapon, and Brum’korath is already on their map.”

The absolute, stoic certainty in the boy's voice paralyzed the council. Elder Gorla leaned forward, her hands trembling slightly against the granite table. The theological implications of his words perfectly mirrored the forbidden prophecies she secretly guarded.

Elder Valka did not strike her gavel. The icy calculation in her blue eyes hardened, boring straight through Thomas and locking onto Lucas. She leaned forward, resting her heavy, ringed palms flat against the black granite.

“Before that titan breached the inner sanctum,” Valka stated, her voice dropping into a low, terrifying frequency that vibrated through the chamber, “our surviving captains recorded the words it bellowed into the dust. It demanded: ‘Bring me the weapon against the Empire.’ It ignored our vaults. It ignored our armories. It tore a direct chasm through our infrastructure toward one specific vector: you.”

She shifted her gaze across the three prisoners, her fingers tapping a slow, deliberate cadence on the slate ledger. “Our deepest archives hold transcripts translated from archaic Nythari stones—imperfect, damaged records where the syntax blurs between an ancient ‘primordial beast’ and a ‘cosmic cataclysm.’ Those texts record three harbingers—the Sent Ones—who would seek the bedrock of this mountain and the steel of dwarven iron to survive an existential purge. I treated those fragments as religious poetry. Fables whispered in the dark.”

Valka’s gaze hardened, her eyes cold and sharp. “A beast falling from the heavens is a tragedy. But a creature tearing through our gates to demand the surrender of three outsiders now standing in chains before this council is no coincidence. Give me the truth, boy. Who forged that monstrosity, why did it target our mountain, and what was it sent here to destroy?”

Lucas met her stare, his voice steady despite the exhaustion clawing at his chest. He offered no false arrogance, only the raw, grounded facts they had bled to uncover.

“We have told you the truth,” Lucas answered, the iron chains rattling softly as he took half a step forward. “I do not know the name of whatever forged that creature, nor do I easily put my faith in ancient fables. All we have are the fragments your own records and the Sent Ones preserved—warnings of an ancient Empire that once threatened this world. I wanted to dismiss it as superstition, but when that beast tore through your gates and demanded the ‘weapon against the Empire,’ coincidence stopped making sense. It did not strike for dwarven gold or territory. Everything points to one conclusion: it came to destroy us before we can even understand what we are.”

He held Valka’s gaze, his tone softening with an earnest, urgent gravity. “Your soldiers died defending their home, and we nearly burned our lives to ash helping them hold the line. We never asked to be the targets of this war, Elder. But if that beast was only an advance strike, more will follow. We cannot survive what is coming if we bleed each other dry in the dark. We need your help. We need your wisdom, your iron, and your understanding.”

A suffocating silence clamped down upon the hall. The elders sat frozen, the crushing weight of the equation locking together in their minds. One plus one yielded two. The fables were dead; the cosmic war had arrived at their gates.

Valka stared at Lucas, the complex, political architecture of her city rapidly collapsing under the staggering weight of their revelation. She slowly lifted her heavy, iron-bound gavel, her knuckles white.

“Your claims strike at the very bedrock of our history,” Valka pronounced, her voice tight with an icy dread she could barely conceal. “The council will withdraw to weigh the truth of your words. If you have lied to excuse your destruction, the executioner's block will be your final destination. Remove them.”

The heavy iron guards swarmed forward, seizing the chains and dragging the trio backward through the cavernous hall. Lucas locked eyes with Gorla for a fleeting microsecond. Her expression was a terrifying mixture of absolute terror and desperate hope. The geopolitical tectonic plates of the world were violently shifting, and as the heavy timber doors slammed shut, plunging them back into the dark corridor, Lucas knew their execution had only been delayed. The true trial was just beginning.

Chapter 16 - Part 2: Judgment in the Halls

Trion-cres, Borin 1772 HSC

The Justice Hall of Brum'korath functioned as an architectural manifestation of unyielding, absolute pressure. Carved directly into the mountain’s sheer granite face, the soaring space was a sweeping testament to dwarven craftsmanship and their relentless commitment to systemic order. The sheer, towering walls were etched deeply with the ancient symbols of terrestrial law—balanced scales, heavy hammers, and the unbroken iron chains of justice. Endless rows of stone benches, filled entirely with somber, calculating dwarves, lined the periphery of the chamber. Above the mass of spectators loomed the elevated, fortified seats of the council, casting an imposing, downward gravity on the floor below. At the absolute center of this acoustic void, illuminated by the piercing, cold radiation of a massive gemstone chandelier, stood Goldar.

The once-imposing leader of the Sent Ones had been systematically stripped of his thick, ceremonial armor and the luxurious vestments of his office. He now wore a coarse, unadorned gray tunic. His thick wrists were bound with heavy iron shackles, the chains bolted securely to a bronze anchor embedded in the bedrock. Despite his drastically diminished physical state and the bruises mottling his face, he radiated a quiet, tectonic strength. His dark eyes scanned the elevated council members, projecting a measured, unbreakable resolve that challenged the very stone of the room.

“Goldar, former High Cleric of the Sent Ones,” the grizzled council leader, Elder Vane, began, his voice generating a heavy, reverberating boom that echoed throughout the vaulted hall. “You stand accused of mass conspiracy, the reckless endangerment of Brum’korath’s civilian infrastructure, and actively harboring anomalous forces that threatened the survival of this entire city. The charges brought against you carry the weight of execution. State your plea to the bedrock.”

Goldar raised his chin, his posture an immovable pillar. “I claim zero guilt regarding conspiracy or malicious intent against my own people,” the dwarf stated, his voice a steady, grinding rumble. “However, I embrace the absolute reality that my actions—and my failures of oversight—have invited devastating suffering into these streets. For the blood spilled, I bear the entire weight of responsibility.”

A frantic, chaotic murmur rippled through the hall. The dwarves in attendance leaned forward, their collective body heat and whispered judgments spiking the ambient tension of the room.

Elder Vane frowned, his golden-braided beard shifting as his jaw tightened. “You speak in riddles, Goldar. You claim the full weight of the blood on our streets, yet you reject the guilt. Reconcile that contradiction before this stone.”

Goldar took a slow, deep breath, pulling the freezing air deep into his lungs. “The Cult of the Sent Ones has existed in the dark for centuries, dedicated solely to guarding a terrible knowledge that predates the foundation of your great city. Our absolute directive is to prepare this world for the catastrophic threats foretold in the ancient Nythari runic tablets—including the descent of the Empire’s Disciples. I acknowledge that we failed to contain the fractured elements within our own ranks. Treason festered in the dark. Fatal mistakes were executed. But our core purpose has always been to construct a shield for this world, to brace the mountain for an impact you refused to believe was coming.”

A second, significantly louder wave of murmurs crashed through the spectators. The council members exchanged sharp, unreadable glances, communicating entirely through rigid shifts in posture.

“Protecting the world?” a younger, fiercely ambitious council member scoffed, leaning aggressively over the granite table. “You protected us by summoning absolute, unfiltered chaos to our very gates? By harboring volatile anomalies who shatter the peace and unleash geological destruction upon our merchant tiers?”

Goldar’s gaze hardened into pure flint. “We did not summon the Disciple. That monstrosity was a living siege-engine forged by the Central Galactic Empire, drawn to this world by forces operating far beyond our borders. And when that star-born calamity breached our walls, we did not hide behind locked doors. We bled in the streets alongside your militia to shatter it.”

Elder Vane raised a heavy, iron-ringed hand, instantly silencing the room with the gesture. “You fought, yes. We acknowledge the ash on your hands. But you also built a fortress of secrets—secrets that allowed a rot to fester in our lower levels. Tell me, Goldar, what of the ideological fracture within your cult? What of the Unbound mercenaries spilling blood in the alleys? Why were the Sent Ones so severely compromised that you could not even trust the vanguards marching in your own shadow?”

For the first time since the trial began, the tectonic foundation of Goldar’s posture visibly cracked. His broad shoulders slumped, the crushing weight of his failure finally breaking through his pride. “The Sent Ones are fractured,” he admitted, the syllables tasting like ash in his mouth. “The burden of the impending prophecy was heavier than I could carry alone. I shared my authority. I placed my faith in lieutenants sworn to our sacred oaths. A faction of those men twisted that trust into an appetite for slaughter, and the cost was catastrophic. I... misjudged the rot in their hearts.”

“You misjudged?” the younger council member pressed, his voice dripping with venomous skepticism. “Or did you close your eyes to the treason, desperate to maintain your iron grip on the deep tunnels until the mountain cracked wide open?”

Goldar’s heavy fists clenched against his iron restraints, the metal groaning softly. “You attempt to compress centuries of silent, agonizing vigilance into a single, brutal moment of failure. Cast your judgment on my flesh if you require a scapegoat, but do not ignore the apocalyptic threat currently orbiting our world. The Empire is awake. Their Disciples operate on a scale of devastation that makes our internal politics entirely irrelevant. The arcane knowledge locked in our archives remains your only viable path to salvation.”

The cavernous chamber fell completely silent. The sheer, terrifying scale of the threat hung over the room like an unexploded bomb.

Elder Vane leaned back into his carved throne, stroking his braided beard thoughtfully, his eyes narrowing into calculated slits. “You brandish knowledge as a shield. Or perhaps, as manipulation. You preach of salvation, yet your historical footprint suggests a deep obsession with self-interest. The Disciple brought absolute ruin to our infrastructure, and the timing of your cult’s mobilization mirrored its descent perfectly. If your mission possesses the profound nobility you claim, why does every action you take reek of clandestine deceit?”

Goldar met the grizzled leader’s gaze with unflinching, heavy gravity. “Secrecy is a shield, Vane, not treachery. The Sent Ones have always stood as guardians over forces that would tear this world to ash if left unchained. Would you have us parade ancient, world-shattering relics before a populace that panics at the sound of thunder? Would you place cataclysmic power in the hands of councilors who cannot see past their quarterly ledgers?”

Vane let the question hang in the freezing air before offering a slow, measured nod. “Your logic possesses a certain structural integrity, Goldar. But eloquence does not reverse the pulverized stone or resurrect the dead. This council must place your stated intentions on the scales against the absolute physical damage your cult has permitted. We require further deliberation before we strike the anvil and render our final judgment.”

Goldar inclined his head, his stoic composure perfectly restored. “I request only that you weigh your verdict against the trajectory of the future, rather than locking your vision entirely on the ashes of the past.”

Vane issued a sharp, final gesture. The heavy armored guards moved instantly, seizing Goldar’s chains and hauling the former High Cleric away toward the deep isolation vaults. As the prisoner vanished into the shadows, the acoustic void of the hall fractured completely. The murmurs of the crowd spiked into a chaotic, overlapping storm of aggressive condemnation and grudging, terrified respect.

Standing heavily guarded in the peripheral shadows of the chamber, Lucas, Mina, and Thomas processed the exchange in absolute silence. The weight of Goldar’s defense—and the council’s unyielding skepticism—pressed against them like a physical force.

“They’re building a scaffold,” Thomas muttered under his breath, his voice a low, heavy rumble. “They need an execution. Something public to keep the city from tearing itself apart.”

Lucas gave a tight nod, his jaw set. “They’ve already made up their minds. If they let him walk, the militia riots. They’re just deciding how clean to make the cut.”

Mina leaned back against the cold stone, resting a hand over her bruised ribs. Her breath came in short, careful drafts, but her eyes were sharp. “If Goldar is right about the prophecy, that monster might only be the first envoy—the start of a whole cascade. If the council wipes out the Sent Ones, we lose our only way down into the vaults. We need to get into those archives before the mountain buries them.”

The heavy bronze doors groaned open, and the guards shoved the three of them back into the corridor. Goldar was left behind closed doors to face the council, but the damage was already done. The trial had lit a short fuse, and the entire city was about to feel the blast.

The corridors outside the Justice Hall were thick with an uneasy, fractured tension as the guards escorted the three of them back down toward the holding tiers. The trial had split the militia right down the middle. To the palace officers and rear-line sentinels who had only seen the aftermath, the outsiders were terrifying anomalies who had brought ruin to the mountain. But among the frontline veterans—especially the battered infantry who had stood behind Thomas’s shield during the avenue slaughter—the mood was completely different. Several bloodstained guards walked with loose grips on their weapons, offering Thomas quiet, respectful nods as they passed, their loyalty firmly anchored to the human boy who had kept them alive when the ground broke.

“We can’t just sit on our hands,” Thomas muttered under his breath, his dark eyes tracking the side halls and counting the guards. “The council is just stalling for time. We need a way out before they make up their minds to lock us away for good.”

Mina nodded grimly. The heavy, suspicious glares from passing dwarves pressed in on all sides. The entire city felt ready to snap, caught between the stubborn elders and the violence spreading from the alleys. Every step felt like crossing thin ice, just waiting for the freeze to give way.

“We don’t have any leverage left,” Lucas murmured, keeping his eyes on the floor as he felt the muffled, anxious thoughts echoing through the walls. “The trial just showed how broken this place really is. The militia hates the Sent Ones, but they have no idea how deep the Unbound have already dug into their own ranks.”

As they rounded a wide stone corner lit by flickering lanterns, they spotted a small, hurried cluster of cloaked dwarves carrying armfuls of bundled scrolls. Standing in the middle of them was Dira.

Mina halted, her hand dropping instinctively toward her belt. “Why is she walking free?”

The terrified girl who had cowered in the sewers was barely recognizable beneath the crushing weight of her new duties. Pinned to the rough leather of Dira's coat was an iron crest—Torgar’s personal vanguard seal. Ever since the Disciple tore through the Bastion yesterday, the younger scribes had worked under her direction, digging through the smoking rubble through the night to salvage what was left. Whatever suspicion had lingered over her past was giving way to a quiet, grudging respect—earned through hours of backbreaking labor without a wink of sleep, and their unyielding reverence for Torgar’s command. With Goldar in chains and senior clerics dead or scattered, Torgar had staked the order's surviving records on her simply because she was the only one left who knew how to navigate the deep archives, and the acolytes around her had rallied to the task.

Lucas didn't leave her loyalty to chance. He dropped his mental firewalls, reaching past the surface static to dive directly into the storm of Dira's mind.

Her thoughts were a chaotic, swirling mess of panic, and Lucas had to actively filter through the noise to isolate the truth. Right at the surface was a sharp jolt of flustered embarrassment—she knew the trio was being held in the hall for the trial, but she had been desperately hoping to avoid running into them in the corridor, terrified of facing their eyes after what happened in the sewers. Sifting deeper, Lucas hit a thick vein of genuine, agonizing shame. The memory of Wallace bleeding from the venom still haunted her; she had been coerced under the Unbound's knives, but she had never wanted the trio harmed, and the urge to make amends was eating her alive.

While Lucas stood motionless, his dark eyes vacant and glazed as his consciousness combed through her mind, an awkward, suffocating silence stretched across the physical corridor. Dira shifted under the weight of the heavy scrolls in her arms, her gaze darting uncomfortably between the stone floor and Mina's sharp, unblinking glare.

“I... I didn’t think I’d run into you here,” Dira stammered softly, her voice barely carrying over the distant murmur of the hall. “I thought the guards were keeping you in the lower tiers.”

“And you were hoping we’d stay down there?” Mina asked, crossing her arms, her tone carrying the sharp, lingering sting of the sewer ambush. “You look like you're ready to drop those books and run again.”

“No! No, I’m not running,” Dira whispered hurriedly, her cheeks burning beneath the soot. She hugged the bundled parchment tightly against her chest like armor. “I know what you must think of me. After what happened with the beast... I thought Wallace was going to die. I couldn't sleep all night. I’m truly sorry.”

“Wallace is alive,” Thomas rumbled, his deep voice cutting through her mounting panic as his eyes tracked the militia guards watching them from the corner. “He's resting in the clinic. But you’re wearing Torgar’s crest. That doesn’t happen by accident.”

Dira swallowed hard, looking down at the heavy ledgers. “Because there's no one else left who knows how to read them. Goldar kept the deep ciphers to himself. I'm the only scribe alive who can translate the ancient tablets.”

Beneath the guilt lay the real reason Torgar had trusted her with his seal. Intertwined with her fear was an irreplaceable vault of knowledge—she was the only surviving scholar who truly understood the archaic dialects of the prophecy and the buried history of the Sent Ones. Mixed into that scholarship was critical, dangerous intel on how the Unbound operated in the dark. She knew her only hope of surviving Thrainor Blackstone’s assassins was to make herself indispensable to the Sent Ones, earning the order's protection by helping them weather the storm.

Lucas severed the probe, his thoughts steady as he confirmed her intent. She's clean, he projected to Mina and Thomas. Her head is an absolute mess of guilt, but she's not a threat. She's ashamed of what happened in the sewers, she has real intel on the Unbound, and she's the only one left who knows how to read the prophecy. Torgar needs her just as much as she needs his shield.

As Lucas blinked, the vacant, glassy stare fading from his dark eyes as his focus snapped back to the hallway, Dira froze mid-breath. A faint shudder ran through her shoulders. She recognized that unblinking, hollow gaze—and the ghostly, fading pressure behind her temples—from the moment he had cracked her mind open in the sewer tunnels. A deep blush of mortification crept up her neck under the soot; she realized he had just sifted through every private, humiliating corner of her thoughts. But seeing the subtle, grounding nod Lucas gave to his companions, she also understood that her truth had been accepted. She was completely exposed, but she was believed.

Swallowing hard, Dira stepped in closer, her voice dropping to a harsh, conspiratorial whisper to keep clear of the militia escorts lingering near the corner.

“The council’s tribunal is just the public theater,” Dira hissed, the words rushing out in a tight, desperate breath. “The real blow landed this morning on the council floor. Under the smoke of the crater, Elder Vane formally introduced the Sovereign Oversight Bill. When the magistrates vote it into law, the independent status of the temples is dead. Every religious faction in this mountain—the Sent Ones, the Unbound, every deep-shrine order—will have to answer directly to the secular government. We’ll be forced to open our archives to state inspectors, register every member, and surrender our vaults to the Ministry of Justice.”

Lucas’s eyes narrowed, the political calculus snapping into place. “They’re using the disaster to nationalize the temples. If you refuse, you’re branded traitors. If you comply, you become government clerks.”

“Exactly,” Dira said, glancing nervously down the corridor. “The vote is scheduled once the cleanup concludes. That’s why the Unbound are moving so violently. They planted sleeper agents across the guard years ago, and this law is a death sentence for their shadows. They aren’t just fighting us anymore—they are preparing to stage a coup before the council can vote away their freedom.”

Mina’s hands clenched into tight fists, the raw creation energy in her blood humming with aggressive rejection of the impending slaughter. “We fought that titan to keep this city standing. If the Unbound weaponize the panic to seize control, thousands of innocent dwarves are going to bleed out in the dark.”

“Then we don't sit here waiting to get hit,” Thomas rumbled, his boots planting firmly against the flagstones. “Whatever sent that monster is still out there hunting us. If the Unbound tear this city apart from the inside, this whole mountain becomes an open grave.”

Dira looked at the massive boy, a bitter, cynical smile touching her lips. “The Unbound don't see this as a disaster. They see it as their chance. They tell everyone they're breaking the old chains—the clans and ancient laws that have kept our folk trapped in these mines for a thousand years. They preach that the Sent Ones are just an old lie that needs to be torn out by the roots. They want to burn down the high halls and rule whatever is left of the ash.”

“They want a slaughter,” Thomas said, shaking his head at the madness of it. “And they'll drown this whole city in blood to get what they want.”

“They will,” Dira whispered, shivering in the cold corridor. “And the younger dwarves are listening to them. Desperate people looking for a way out. If the Unbound pull this off, they won't just kill the council—they will tear this mountain apart from the inside out.”

The gravity of Dira’s intelligence settled over the group like a suffocating blanket of lead. The trial of Goldar Ironfist was entirely irrelevant. The mountain was actively consuming itself, and the Unbound were the parasites driving the rot.

“So what’s the plan?” Mina asked, locking her green eyes onto Lucas, her jaw tight with restless tension.

Lucas met her gaze, his mind already cutting through the chaos. “We find who we can actually trust. We root out the traitors in the guard, and we hit the Unbound before they tear this place down. If this mountain falls, the Unbound take the deep vaults, the Central Lands march their armies in to lock down the passes, and the whole continent gets dragged into a war it won't survive—especially with whatever dropped that monster still watching from the dark.”

Dira let out a bitter, exhausted breath, her knuckles white around her leather ledger. “That sounds clean when you say it fast, Lucas. But you have no idea how buried we actually are.” She pressed a trembling hand to her face, dark circles heavy beneath her eyes. “Goldar is in chains. Torgar is drowning just trying to stop our surviving fighters from tearing each other apart in the lower wards, and half the elders won't even look at me after what happened in the tunnels. I’m a scribe, not a spymaster. I’m trying to hold together what’s left of our records with shaking hands while the council votes to outlaw us.”

She looked between the three of them, her voice dropping to a harsh, desperate whisper. “I can try to reach the few elders who haven't fled or turned. But don't pretend we have an army ready to march on your word. We're a broken house, and the Unbound are already inside the walls.”

As they turned to head back down toward the holding cells, the lead militia guard stepped directly into their path, his hand resting heavily on the pommel of his broadsword.

“Your leash is short,” the guard growled, his voice a flat, ugly threat. “Don't think for a second we've forgotten the blood in the streets or the rubble you left behind. Take one wrong step in these halls, and I'll take your heads myself, council be damned.”

The atmospheric pressure in the corridor reached a lethal peak. Lucas, Mina, and Thomas resumed their walk, their faces entirely devoid of fear, projecting only a cold, unified resolve. The city of Brum'korath was standing on the absolute edge of the abyss, and they were the only force heavy enough to anchor it.

Deep within the secured medical wards of the dwarven stronghold, Wallace was slowly clawing his way back from the brink. The dwarven poultices had finally stopped the black rot spreading from the beast’s bite, and the fever burning through his veins was beginning to break. But he was far from safe. Four heavily armed militia guards stood watch over his bed, their hands never straying far from their axes. His presence had set the whole ward on edge. Tense whispers drifted past his cot—some claimed he was a secret agent pulling strings for the Sent Ones, while paranoid officers suspected he was an Unbound assassin sent to slit throats in the dark. Through it all, Wallace lay completely still, breathing in slow, measured rhythms to feign unconsciousness. Behind his closed eyes, he tracked the heavy scrape of boots, counted the minutes between guard shifts, and memorized every creak in the stone floor. He had survived far worse holding cells than this, and he would be ready when the time came to slip the leash.

The holding chamber assigned to them was a stark, geometric vault of sheer gray stone. The heavy timber door was secured from the outside by a massive iron deadbolt. A small, grated hearth radiated a weak, localized thermal heat in the far corner, doing little to combat the pervasive, bone-deep chill of the mountain. They were guests of the council, but the architecture of the room served the exact same function as a high-security cell.

Mina sat on the edge of a rigid stone cot near the fire, rolling her shoulders to work out the lingering stiffness in her side. Her natural vitality had already cleared the worst of the damage—the scrape at her temple had closed cleanly, and the mild concussion from being thrown into the rubble had faded into a dull ache. She was bruised and sore along her ribs where the impact had caught her, but the dwarven salves and her own rushing heat had done their work. She was back on her feet, restless, and itching for open air.

Lucas sat on a small wooden stool on the opposing side of the hearth. His dark eyes were unfocused, staring into the flickering embers while his synthesis mind rapidly churned through the compounding variables. Thomas paced the strict perimeter of the room, his heavy boots striking the flagstones in a slow, rhythmic, tectonic beat that anchored the chaotic energy of the space.

“We can’t just sit in this room waiting for them to decide what to do with us,” Mina said, breaking the heavy silence. She kicked a stray pebble across the flagstones, her voice tight with restless energy.

Lucas pulled his eyes away from the hearth, blinking against the embers. “I know. Staying here is a dead end. We're cornered, and the longer we wait, the worse our odds get.”

Thomas stopped his patrol, his heavy boots settling firmly against the stone. “The cult is in pieces, the militia is ready to lock down the mountain, and the Unbound are running the alleys. If we’re going to make a move, we need to know exactly what we’re hitting.”

Mina let out a slow, steady breath, trying to keep the restless heat in her chest under control. “I just need a target. The Unbound are hiding behind the riots. If we sit here waiting for the council to make a decision, we’re just waiting for someone to slide a blade between our ribs in the dark.”

Lucas’s gaze hardened. He felt the exact same suffocating walls closing in. The Unbound were creeping through the lower levels of the mountain, and staying linked to the Sent Ones meant they were painted with targets.

“We don’t let them corner us,” Lucas said quietly, cold certainty settling into his voice as his fingers brushed the hilt of his belt knife. “We hit them before they find us.”

Mina watched his rigid posture, feeling the quiet, dangerous focus sharpening in his thoughts. Reaching out through the invisible mental bond between them, she spoke directly into his mind.

You’re thinking about the deep temple, she projected, her thoughts a warm, urgent current brushing against his. You think the Unbound are going after whatever is buried in those vaults.

Lucas met her eyes across the room, the sharp tension in his face softening as her presence grounded him. Yeah. And Blackstone isn't the only one looking for it, he answered, his thoughts sharp and focused. The council wants to seize the vaults, the World Police are waiting to tear this place apart, and the Unbound want to burn the Sent Ones' history to the ground. If they destroy whatever is buried in that temple, they erase the only proof that the Empire was ever here.

Mina felt the quiet, steadying comfort of their bond settle over her chest. Dira was right about them. If the wrong hands get down there first, the truth is gone for good. But we can't just sneak down to the deep vaults on our own—the militia is crawling all over the lower tunnels.

We move carefully, Lucas agreed. If Torgar and his fighters draw the guards' attention, we slip down to the temple on our own. We find what's down there first.

The quiet understanding settled between them, firm and unbroken.

Before either of them could say another word, three sharp, measured knocks rattled against the heavy timber door. It wasn't the violent banging of a militia raid—it was steady and deliberate. Lucas stood up from his stool, his focus sharpening instantly.

“Stay ready,” Lucas whispered, stepping quietly away from the hearth.

Thomas stepped in front of the entrance, his broad shoulders squaring as he planted his heavy frame between the door and the room. The timber groaned open, revealing an armed dwarven sentinel standing in the corridor. Behind the guard stepped Torgar. The vanguard of the Sent Ones looked exactly as he had in the ruined courtyard—calm, deliberate, yet carrying a newly forged, suffocating tension.

“I need to speak with you,” Torgar stated, his deep voice low and urgent as his eyes swept over the three teenagers.

Lucas stared at the dwarven cleric, his dark eyes sharp with suspicion. He glanced past Torgar at the militia guard who had simply stood aside to let him in. It made no sense. Goldar had just been dragged off to a dungeon in chains, and the council was actively drafting laws to outlaw their entire religion. Why was the vanguard's commander walking through the Justice Hall without iron on his wrists?

“How are you walking free in these halls?” Lucas asked, his voice cold and direct. “Your High Cleric is facing the executioner's block and the council is hunting your people. Why aren't you in a cell?”

Torgar stepped fully into the room, pulling the heavy timber door shut to seal out the corridor. “Because the council is terrified of what happens if they lock up every leader at once. They need someone keeping our surviving fighters from burning down the lower tiers while they argue over their new laws. They gave me temporary clearance to maintain order—but that leash is running out fast.”

The dwarf drew a heavy, gravelly breath, looking between Lucas and Mina with unvarnished desperation. “The Sent Ones are tearing themselves apart from the inside. The council granted you a temporary stay, but the elders demanding our blood grow louder by the hour. I need your help. The order is standing on the edge of an open grave, and if we don’t hold the line, the Unbound will butcher whatever is left of us in the dark.”

“Hold the line?” Thomas rumbled, his voice thick with blunt suspicion. “You want us to go out there and play saviors for your cult after everything that happened in Kingston?”

Torgar’s gaze remained rock-steady, though a faint, highly suppressed flicker of uncertainty broke his stoic facade. “The city is fracturing. Goldar’s public tribunal inflicted terminal damage to our credibility. But if we execute a unified, highly visible counter-offensive against the Unbound, I can rally the remaining loyalists. We need your raw power to restore our tactical superiority.”

Mina exchanged a sharp, loaded glance with Lucas. He’s trying to use our name to hold onto his command, she projected, a bitter taste in her mouth. He wants us standing in front of his fighters so they don't lose their nerve.

Lucas leaned back against the stone, his face completely still as he reached toward Torgar’s mind to listen for a lie. He caught the raw surface pressure—the genuine, suffocating dread of a commander watching his people get slaughtered in the dark. But when Lucas tried to push deeper to see what was hidden beneath, he slammed straight into that familiar, unyielding wall of stone-trained discipline. Torgar’s brow furrowed slightly, his dark eyes narrowing as he felt the faint, probing pressure against his temples. The cleric didn’t flinch; he simply held Lucas’s gaze, perfectly aware the boy was testing his defenses again.

Lucas pulled his mind back, the dull resistance leaving a faint ache behind his eyes. He's blocking me, he projected to Mina. I felt his surface thoughts—he’s genuinely terrified for his people, and he's desperate. But he locked the rest behind that mental shield. He’s holding something back, but his need for our help is real.

Mina stepped forward, her hand resting firmly against Lucas’s arm. Then we work with him for now. We could find our way back to the temple through the sewers or even from Tredmor, but having Torgar’s fighters will keep the guards off our backs—and once we're actually inside that temple, we'll need someone who knows the layout.

Torgar looked at them, his heavy, armored chest rising with a deep breath. “I offer you a mutually beneficial pact. Help me rebuild the wall, and I will ensure the city council grants you total amnesty. The survival of Brum'korath depends on our immediate cooperation.”

Lucas stared at the dwarven cleric, feeling the heavy, conflicting weight of the choice. Deep down, a part of him still desperately hoped the prophecy was a flawed equation—that the Disciple had been an isolated nightmare, and that no other monsters were waiting in the dark to hunt them. But looking at the deep lines of grief carved into Torgar’s face, Lucas understood the cleric's perspective. To these dwarves, the ancient warnings were an absolute, terrifying reality, and Torgar was simply clutching at whatever hope was left to save his people.

“We’ll work with you,” Lucas said, his voice quiet, firm, and stripped of false bravado. “We want to keep this city from falling apart just as much as you do. But understand this, Torgar: we aren't tools to be used by your order, and we aren't bait for your enemies. If we find out the Unbound are playing you, or if you try to manipulate us, this deal is over.”

Torgar’s lips tightened into a grim, acknowledging line. “The terms are acceptable. My focus is entirely on preserving the Sent Ones. I require your strength to execute the purge.”

The conversation terminated with an abrupt, chilling silence. Torgar offered a stiff bow and exited the chamber, leaving the heavy door to click shut behind him.

Lucas, Mina, and Thomas stood in the quiet of the stone room, the heavy weight of the choice settling over them.

“We’re walking on thin ice,” Thomas rumbled, leaning back against the rough wall. “If this deal goes south, we lose the only cover we have left in this mountain. But sitting here waiting for the council to decide our fate isn't an option.”

“No, it isn't,” Lucas said quietly, his gaze fixed on the heavy timber door. “And we aren't waiting blind.”

Over the hours they had spent locked in the Justice Hall, Lucas had kept his mind quietly active, reaching through the stone walls to brush against every guard, clerk, and courier who passed within range. The sentinels didn't know high-level council secrets, but their thoughts held practical pieces of the ground: shift schedules, blind spots along the lower stairwells, and the exact route connecting this holding tier to the sewer access tunnels. He had also caught scattered surface chatter—whispers of extra militia arriving at the upper gates and growing panic over the Unbound's movements in the alleys.

It gave them a way out. If Torgar’s alliance fell apart or the council sent guards to drag them to the block, they wouldn't sit and wait. They had the patrol timings memorized, and they were fully prepared to take down the sentinels at the door and fight their way into the dark on their own.

As the hearth fire burned low, casting long, fading shadows across the stone, the three of them quietly went over the escape route. The trial of Goldar was already fading into the background. Torgar and his surviving clerics were clinging to them for survival, but Lucas, Mina, and Thomas knew the real test was waiting beneath the city—reaching those buried vaults before anyone else could beat them to it.

Chapter 16 - Part 3: Echoes of the Trial

Quadra-cres, Borin 1772 HSC

The high diplomatic chambers of Brum’korath rose like an unyielding fortress of stone and law. Carved deep into the mountain’s upper tier, the hall bore the crushing weight of centuries of unbroken dwarven rule. Towering basalt pillars and severe masonry stood as a permanent testament to the clan elders' rigid authority. Lucas, Mina, and Thomas stood shoulder-to-shoulder before the elevated crescent table of magistrates. The air in the chamber hung thick and suffocating, charged with the lethal tension of a tribunal weighing survival against political power.

An official demand from Kingston had arrived at the mountain gates the previous evening. Carried by a grim-faced envoy under the authority of the Central Lands, the decree was an ultimatum. The World Police demanded the immediate surrender and extradition of the fugitives, citing their direct involvement in the catastrophic explosion in Kingston Square, the breach and robbery of the municipal magi-tech vault, and their classification as dangerous, unregistered biological anomalies fleeing Central law.

To Mina, the decree felt like a noose drawing tight around her throat. An untamed, restless heat flared in her blood at the thought of being dragged back to the sterile cages of the capital. To Thomas, the demand was a bitter insult to the blood and bone they had spent holding the line to save this city from being crushed. To Lucas, it was a brutal fracture in their plans—a wall thrown up across the only narrow path they had left to stay alive.

“We understand you have questions to ask,” Elder Vane rumbled, his deep voice carrying the heavy resonance of stone across the chamber. “However, our authority in these peaks is absolute. The bedrock of Brum'korath answers only to this council. We take no orders from Kingston.”

The grizzled magistrate’s words were aimed squarely at the World Police representative seated rigidly at the edge of the dais. Officer Denka projected the cold, polished authority of the Central Lands. Her sharp, severe features and immaculate dark uniform stood in stark contrast to the soot and rough stone of the dwarven hall.

“We are offering cooperation, Elder, not orders,” Denka replied, her voice smooth and deliberate. “Yet these three are fugitives wanted across the Central Lands for the destruction of Kingston Square and the breach of our municipal vaults. The devastation in your streets only confirms what our analysts already concluded: they are volatile, weaponized anomalies who cannot be contained by local militias. The World Police has the specialized facilities to secure them. They belong in our custody.”

“They have already answered to the stone,” Vane countered, his heavy hands gripping the edge of the granite table. “They used their strange power to fight the corrupt elements tearing this city apart. They held the line when our own walls were falling. Consequently, they remain under our guard until our own inquiry is finished.”

“An indefinite delay,” Denka countered, her eyes narrowing. “The Central Lands are watching the smoke rise from your peaks, Elder. Your laws will mean very little if the capital decides you are harboring fugitives who threaten the entire realm.”

Lucas felt Mina’s entire frame stiffen beside him. Her hand pressed lightly against her bruised ribs, her breathing tight with anger. Before she could speak, Thomas stepped forward, his broad shoulders planting a solid wall between his friends and the dais.

“We stayed in the street,” Thomas said, his voice a blunt, heavy rumble that filled the hall. “We bled alongside the militia to keep this city from caving in. If we had run, the mercenaries and that monster would have turned this entire mountain into a mass grave. If your police force needs someone to blame, go hunt whatever dropped that beast out of the sky instead of the people who killed it.”

A heavy silence settled over the room. The dwarven magistrates exchanged quiet, meaningful glances. Officer Denka’s jaw tightened, her posture rigid under the boy's challenge.

Elder Vane leaned forward, resting his palms flat on the granite. “This discussion is over. Under the decree introduced to our floor this morning, all religious orders, their archives, and their associates fall under our direct authority. These three remain in our custody until our investigation concludes. We officially reject your extradition request.”

Denka’s lips thinned into a pale, dissatisfied line. She rose from her seat, smoothing the crisp lapels of her uniform with practiced, icy restraint. “I will transmit your refusal to the High Command. Consider the weight of this decision, Elder. The capital's patience is not endless.”

Her heavy boots struck the polished stone floor in a sharp, rhythmic cadence as she exited the chamber. The immediate threat of extradition receded with her departure, but the crushing pressure left in her wake lingered. The council’s scrutiny felt like a vice clamping down around Lucas's skull.

Elder Vane shifted his heavy gaze toward the shadows near the primary archway. Wallace stood apart from the trio, his posture immaculate and disciplined, masking the severe poison still burning through his veins.

“Sir Wallace,” Vane addressed the operative, his tone carrying a blunt, practical weight. “The council has set our terms. You will return to the Central Lands as the formal diplomatic envoy representing these three before the Hegemony. In the meantime, they remain in Brum'korath under our direct ward.”

Wallace offered a sharp, polite bow. “The council's terms are accepted. I will serve as their voice before the authorities in Kingston. In return, I hold this council to its word: Miss Mina and her companions must remain safe beneath your roof.”

Vane offered a curt, unyielding nod. “Their safety is guaranteed by dwarven law.”

The council adjourned the session. The heavy, suffocating tension lingered in the air as the party formed a tight cluster, following Wallace out of the chamber and down into the winding, shadowed corridors leading back to their quarters. The chill of the mountain seemed to deepen with every step, the stone walls pressing inward around them. Upon crossing the threshold of their heavy iron door, Wallace turned to face them, his sharp features etched with uncharacteristic gravity.

“Our position is dangerous,” Wallace murmured, keeping his voice low in the quiet room. “But this buys us precious time. Going back to Kingston provides a necessary smokescreen. I will drown the World Police in endless legal disputes and stall their warrants, giving you the room you need to deal with the Unbound.”

“You're leaving us behind,” Mina said, her voice tight with fierce, protective anxiety. The ache in her bruised ribs fueled her frustration, and the thought of losing Wallace’s steady presence sent a wave of raw dread through her chest.

Wallace’s stern face softened, a rare, quiet sorrow showing in his eyes. For a fleeting moment, the disciplined operative slipped away, leaving only the man who had watched her grow up and bled to keep her breathing. “I don't want to leave you, Mina,” he murmured softly. “You know that. But sitting in this cage beside you won't keep you safe. Out there, I can buy you time. I can stall the police in Kingston, work with your uncle, and keep the capital from knocking down these gates. You three are strong. You're tougher and smarter than anyone in this mountain gives you credit for. I'll fight for you out there, but you have to promise me you'll stay alive down here. The Unbound won't wait, and I won't be here to step in front of the blade.”

Lucas met the operative’s gaze, his jaw locked tight. “The logic is sound. We know what to do.”

Wallace placed a steady, gloved hand on Lucas’s shoulder, offering a firm, grounding grip. “Stay sharp. Every move you make is being watched by the council and the capital alike. Take control of your own fate, Lucas. Do not let them decide who you are.”

The operative turned sharply on his heel, his coat sweeping the stone as he exited the chamber. The heavy timber door clicked shut, leaving the trio sealed within a suffocating, echoing silence.

Mina sank onto the edge of the cot near the grated hearth, her hand instinctively pressing against the bandages wrapped around her ribs. Thomas resumed his steady pacing, his heavy boots scuffing a slow, rhythmic beat against the flagstones. Lucas leaned back against the cold stone, crossing his arms as his mind worked through the dangerous turns ahead.

“Sitting here is a mistake,” Thomas rumbled, his dark eyes locked on the flickering embers. “The council knows we didn't summon that monster, but staying cooped up in a stone box while the Unbound circle in the dark makes us sitting ducks.”

“We aren't just sitting,” Lucas replied quietly, his voice carrying a cold, steady certainty. “We play along with their restrictions to hide our real moves. We stay in our quarters, watch the guard shifts, and find out everything we can about the Unbound and what’s hidden in the Sent Ones' archives.”

Mina looked up, the fierce spark in her green eyes cutting through the gloom. “And when the World Police finally march through the gates to drag us back to Kingston?”

“They’ll find an empty room,” Lucas stated, the freezing certainty in his voice settling over the space. “We find what's buried in the temple, and we break out of this mountain long before their warrants ever reach the council.”

The hearth fire crackled, casting jagged, dancing shadows across their exhausted faces. The waiting had begun, but beneath their quiet compliance, the desperate plans for their escape were already set in stone.

The lower corridors of Brum’korath exuded a heavy, oppressive stillness. The frantic, chaotic energy that had consumed the city during Goldar’s tribunal had solidified into a permanent, paranoid silence. Lucas walked shoulder-to-shoulder with Mina and Thomas, navigating the dimly lit, vaulted halls carved deep into the bedrock. The physical weight of their predicament hung over them, compounding the bone-deep exhaustion that sleep had done nothing to cure.

Mina leaned heavily against Lucas’s shoulder. The restless vitality in her blood was steadily knitting the deep trauma left by the Disciple, but the mending came with a relentless, burning ache. Though the dwarven healers had applied potent salves, her bruised ribs sent a sharp throb through her chest with every breath. Despite the soreness coiling through her frame, she forced her legs to match their pace. The stifling, enclosed air of their secure quarters felt like a tomb; she needed movement to keep the walls from closing in.

“I know why Wallace had to leave,” Thomas muttered, his voice a low, grinding rumble that cut through the silence, heavy with unyielding frustration. “Doesn't mean I like it. Sitting around in these halls is suicide. If whatever sent that monster drops another one on our heads, or if the Unbound send a squad to slit our throats in our sleep, we're cornered.”

Mina shifted her weight, tightening her grip on Lucas’s arm. “Wallace made the right call. Out there, he can throw the police off our scent and tie them up in knots. If he stayed here, he’d just be another target trapped in the dark with us.”

“Maybe,” Thomas said, halting his stride, his heavy fists clenching at his sides. “Doesn't change the mess we're in. We can't fight the Empire, the Unbound, and the city's army all at once.”

“We separate the threats,” Lucas said, his voice dropping to a cold, quiet baseline. He turned to face his friends, his dark eyes sharp with chilling clarity. “The Unbound are street-level parasites. The World Police are tied up in their own red tape. But the core of this disaster traces back to a singular truth. That monster didn't fall on this mountain by chance. It came here to hunt us.”

Mina’s breathing hitched, a restless tremor running through her shoulders as the memory resurfaced. “The second it crashed into the upper tier, I felt it. A suffocating heat pressing right against my skull, pulling straight toward our position. It was locked onto our blood before it even took its first step.”

Lucas turned his gaze to Thomas. “Did you feel it? When it landed?”

Thomas shook his head slowly, his voice a low, heavy rumble. “I felt the bedrock shake. That’s it. No tethers pulling at my head, no strange weight in the air.” He paused, looking down at his calloused hands. “Just stone and dust.”

Mina frowned, her green eyes searching his face. “You didn't feel that pressure at all?”

“It was hunting the magic,” Lucas said quietly, though behind his eyes, the calculation locked into place. He had known since they were twelve that his own mind could never find purchase in Thomas’s thoughts; whatever made Thomas immune to his telepathy had left the beast blind to him as well. “It needed an active current to track. It had our scent, not his.”

“Which fits what that elder asked in the hall,” Thomas pointed out, his voice steady. “He asked if I was the companion from the tablets. The one standing beside the two who carry the fire.”

“Which means the pieces are coming together,” Lucas said, his mind pulling the facts into sharp focus. “The Disciple struck this mountain because we are here—the ‘weapon against the Empire’ it was screaming to destroy. Goldar told us the dwarven tablets were translated from ancient Nythari legends about three figures who fought off the Empire seventeen hundred years ago. If this cult has spent centuries hoarding the history of that first war, then whatever Goldar kept locked in the deep vaults holds the answers we need. The records, the ancient defenses, whatever was preserved from that first conflict.”

Thomas released a heavy, weary sigh, raking a hand through his hair. “We're running out of time. Do we wait around for the dwarven council to realize we're telling the truth? Or do we sit on our hands and pray the Empire takes its time sending the next one?”

“We move first,” Lucas stated, his posture unyielding. “We stop waiting on the council. The Sent Ones' leadership is shattered, but there are still people in their ranks who know the truth. We have the guards bring an archivist from the cult directly to our quarters. Once we have someone who understands the texts inside these walls, we extract what Goldar was hoarding in the dark, and we decode the prophecy before the Empire sends another herald to finish the job.”

Mina absorbed his words, the restless heat in her chest settling into a clear vector. “Then let’s call the guard.”

Thomas stepped to the threshold, rapping his knuckles firmly against the reinforced timber. The viewing grate slid open with a sharp metallic scrape, revealing the impassive eyes of the dwarven sentinel on watch. Thomas stated the request with calm, blunt authority: they needed an archivist from the Sent Ones brought to their quarters with the historical records. Recognizing the reasonable demand of the council's high-profile wards, the guard gave a curt nod and closed the grate to dispatch a runner to the lower archives.

An hour later, the heavy iron deadbolt ground back. The timber door opened, and two armored sentinels ushered Dira across the threshold. She clutched an armful of bundled scrolls and heavy leather-bound ledgers against her chest, her pale face dusted with soot and exhaustion. The guards barked a strict thirty-minute limit, stepped back into the corridor, and sealed the heavy deadbolt behind her.

In the private containment of the room, Dira set the heavy ledgers on the stone table, releasing a shuddering breath. “The wardens told me you demanded an archivist. What has happened?”

“We're done waiting,” Lucas replied, his tone stripped of pretense as he closed the distance. “We need the truth about the prophecy and whatever Goldar was keeping locked in the deep vaults. That titan came hunting the ‘weapon against the Empire’—and if the ancient texts align with what breached our gates, we need the exact metrics of what is buried beneath us.”

Dira looked down at the flagstones, haunted by the fragmented history she guarded. “The prophecy is a tangled mess of ancient riddles. It speaks of a massive upheaval from the stars—primordial forces returning to reshape Hybris. The Sent Ones convinced themselves we were meant to guide that storm. Goldar kept the oldest translations locked away. He hoarded the truth so no one could question his rule.”

“What was he keeping sealed in the depths?” Mina pressed, her voice urgent, leaning over the table.

Dira shook her head slowly, her fingers tracing the cracked leather of an ancient text. “The records are severely damaged. The oldest fragments speak only of sealed chambers carved beneath the original sanctuary—vaults holding secret knowledge or ancient writings from the first founders. Goldar hoarded the ciphers to those deepest chambers, convinced they contained the foundational truth of our origins, but he refused to let any scribe inspect the primary tablets.”

Lucas exchanged a heavy glance with Mina and Thomas. The equation contained too many unknown variables. He had no baseline metric for what lay buried beneath the bedrock—it could be forgotten scribings, corrupted archives, or an empty room. But if Goldar had anchored his entire order to whatever lay sealed in those depths, it remained their only viable vector to calculate why an apocalyptic entity had torn through the mountain to hunt them.

“Then we explore the deep vaults ourselves,” Lucas said, his voice ringing with quiet finality. “Whatever Goldar sealed in the dark, we unearth it. We secure that knowledge and decode the truth before the Empire strikes again.”

Dira met his gaze, her posture tight with a quiet, practiced restraint. Living under the constant surveillance of the Justice Hall’s wardens for days had turned the presence of armed sentinels into an established metric of her routine. “The council already occupies the site,” she stated plainly, adjusting the heavy ledger in her arms. “The militia extracted the coordinates from imprisoned cultists days ago and fortified a permanent military perimeter across the Hidden Temple. If we descend to those vaults, the magistrates will enforce a full armed escort—council observers and heavy iron locked to our formation every step of the way.”

A faint, steady resolve edged into her voice as she looked between the three fugitives. “The militia holds the gates, but their soldiers cannot read the stone. I know the internal glyph syntax and the unmapped bypasses within the sanctum. If the council marches us down under an armed guard, I will decipher the archives before their wardens comprehend what we are uncovering. Whatever records and guidance I have left are yours.”

As the pact was sealed in the shadows, the crushing weight of the mountain settled heavily across their shoulders. Their bodies were battered and their minds strained to the breaking point, but the luxury of rest had run out. The fate of Brum'korath—and the world beyond its peaks—was hanging over the edge of the abyss, and they were the only ones left standing between the stone and the dark.

The atmosphere inside the council chamber of the Sent Ones was thick with a guarded, suffocating tension. Deep within the subterranean headquarters, the surviving elders sat around a heavy table carved from petrified timber, the room lit by the dim glow of embedded crystals. But the sanctuary was no longer their own.

Seated prominently at the table among the clerics was a special envoy from the Justice Hall—a severe, sharp-eyed dwarven magistrate clad in the formal gray coat of the city government, a bronze council seal pinned to his chest. Following the tribunal and the introduction of the emergency oversight decree, the magistrates had forced their way into the temple's inner workings. The envoy was stationed directly in their midst, auditing their ledgers, investigating their remaining assets, and ensuring that every major decision passed under the watchful eye of the city council.

When Lucas, Mina, Thomas, and Dira were escorted into the chamber, the envoy looked up from a stack of slate tablets, his calculating gaze tracking them with cold suspicion. Torgar stood at the head of the table, forced to navigate the council's survival under the magistrate's direct supervision. The dwarven vanguard carried the shattered weight of the order on his shoulders, his eyes meeting the trio's with a mixture of relief and guarded caution.

“We are glad to see you standing,” Torgar said, his deep voice echoing in the quiet room as he addressed the newcomers while remaining painfully aware of the envoy sitting at his elbow.

“We appreciate you speaking up for us at the trial,” Torgar said, addressing the quiet council before turning his eyes back to the three of them. “But right now, we have to pick up the pieces. That titan was only the first strike in something far larger. We cannot afford to stumble around in the dark.”

Lucas gave a stiff nod. The Sent Ones were falling apart, losing ground by the hour, but they still held the records and the access he needed. The prophecy held the answers, and staying alive meant digging them up.

“We aren't here to cause more trouble for your people,” Lucas said, keeping his voice calm and steady in the tense room. “Whatever is happening in this city, the ancient warnings are coming true. The Empire found us once. If we just sit here waiting, they’ll tear this whole mountain apart to wipe us out.”

Torgar's expression hardened with quiet grief. “We fear the exact same thing, Lucas. The Empire is an ancient nightmare, but we won't roll over for them. We held our ground against that beast, and we'll stand firm again. But our backs are against the wall. The trial shattered our alliances. The World Police want someone to blame, and they are building the gallows right outside.”

Mina glanced toward the narrow, reinforced window overlooking the dark stone street below. The shadows outside felt thick and suffocating. The World Police were relentless, and she knew their borrowed time was running out fast.

“So what's the plan?” Thomas demanded, his deep voice cutting through the heavy air. “The city council has us locked down with militia guards watching every breath we take. Do the magistrates really expect us to sit quietly in our quarters until the World Police bust through the gates and drag us away?”

Torgar kept his composure, though frustration shadowed his eyes. “The magistrates are stalling, Thomas,” the cleric said, his voice deep and steady. “The city council is terrified. They think keeping you under armed watch will keep Kingston from marching an army to our doorstep, while they figure out how to deal with the Empire. They are walking a razor's edge, trying not to give the capital an excuse to invade.”

“Sitting on our hands will get us killed,” Lucas said, his voice rising to cut through the quiet hall. “We don't have time to wait for committee meetings or council approvals. Whatever was set in motion is moving faster by the day. We can't stop what's coming, but we can stop hiding and do something about it.”

Torgar gave a slow, heavy nod, recognizing the hard truth in the boy's words. “We will give you whatever help we can,” the cleric said, his gaze briefly drifting toward the envoy across the table. “But you have to understand how narrow our ground is. The Sent Ones are broken and scattered, and the city council is scrutinizing every breath we take. With the magistrates watching our every move, we cannot afford a single mistake.”

Dira stepped forward, her voice cutting through the heavy air with sudden, quiet strength. “We still have people out there, Torgar,” she said, her blue eyes sharp with determination. “Loyal fighters and clerics hiding in the outer tunnels, waiting for word. If the old warnings are real, we call them in right now.”

Torgar looked at the young scribe with a mix of surprise and worry. “You want to bring in the outcasts,” he murmured, weighing the risk. “They walked away from the temple years ago. We can't just command people who refused to follow our rules.”

“They didn't walk away from our faith,” Dira pushed back, refusing to back down. “They walked away from Goldar and his excuses. They've been waiting in the dark for the people spoken of in the songs. And those people are standing right in front of us.”

A profound, echoing silence seized the chamber. The elder council members exchanged long, heavily weighted glances. The sheer gravity of Dira’s proposal threatened to rewrite the entire operational structure of the cult. Lucas observed the internal friction battling behind Torgar’s eyes—the desperate clash between maintaining traditional stability and embracing a radical, necessary evolution.

“Then we have to change the plan,” Torgar finally conceded, his voice heavy with resignation. “I will give the order to open communication with the outcasts. We bring them in, and we face what comes together.”

Mina let out a slow, steady breath. The fragile alliance they were building rested on dangerous compromises. They were walking a narrow line—caught between a broken cult, the watchful eyes of the city militia, and the looming threat of the Empire hanging over the mountain.

Before Torgar could conclude the session, the Justice Hall envoy closed his slate ledger with a sharp, deliberate click. The dwarven magistrate stood, adjusting the bronze seal on his coat as he delivered his officious reminder. “Every decision recorded here—including any proposed contact with unregistered outcasts—remains provisional under the oversight decree. The Justice Hall will review these proceedings and sort out the formal authorizations as soon as possible. Until then, the temple remains under standard council cordon.”

With that bureaucratic stamp hanging over the room, the council dismissed the assembly. Lucas felt a quiet, grim resolve settle into his chest. They had charted a fragile direction, but the real test was waiting for them in the dark tunnels below.

“We get ready,” Lucas said, looking at Mina and Thomas. “We're running out of time.”
